In any case, he will commit to his father and his wife, and he shall be given to him, and he shall be given to him, and he shall not be given to him
Whether by way of a loan, etc. The Tur and Mechaber list all the forms of obligation, but their wording leaves unresolved whether Rabbi Natan's rule applies when the original transfer was by way of a gift. Baal HaTerumot cites authorities who hold that Rabbi Natan does not apply to a gift. At first glance, the Rosh's words in Bava Kamma, in the chapter HaChovel, concerning a married woman who causes damage, appear to indicate the same. The Gemara asks that she should sell her ketubah for its present value, and answers that with respect to her husband she would certainly waive it, etc. The Rosh writes that this applies specifically where she has no nichsei melog or nichsei tzon barzel, but if she has such property she should sell it for its present value. The Shiltei Giborim and Maadanei Melech ask: with respect to nichsei tzon barzel, she has only an ordinary debt against her husband, so why should she not be able to waive it like any other debt? If so, the same concern remains that with respect to her husband she would certainly waive it. The Maadanei Melech thought to answer that she would have no incentive to waive it because she would then have to pay for the loss under the law of garmi. With a ketubah, by contrast, she can waive it because it is forbidden for the husband to live with her without a new ketubah, and he will write her another one, so there is no ultimate loss. This answer has no substance. The Rosh himself later asks how she could waive the ketubah if she would then have to pay for the loss. According to the Maadanei Melech, that question was already answered by the Rosh's own circumstances, since the husband would simply write her another ketubah and she would suffer no loss. Moreover, the Rosh's view, as the Tur cites it, is that under garmi she pays only the amount she received for selling the claim, not its full value. If so, even with nichsei tzon barzel she could arrange to waive the claim. She would pay only the amount for which she sold it, while she and her husband would gain the balance, exactly as Tosafot write there. According to Rabbenu Tam's explanation, that she pays only what she received, the Gemara is readily understood for precisely this reason, because she profits from the difference. The Rosh likewise writes this rationale in the first chapter of Bava Metzia, that she could waive and divide the excess with her husband. The Maadanei Melech himself also noticed that later, where a woman injured her husband, the Gemara establishes the case where her ketubah is not larger than the minimum Torah amount. This implies that where she injured others the rule may apply even when the ketubah is larger, and nevertheless she cannot simply sell the excess because she could waive it to her husband. According to the Maadanei Melech, however, even when she injured others she should sell the excess because she would not waive it, since she would have to pay, and the husband would not need to write her a new ketubah for the amount of the additional ketubah. There is another difficulty. The Rosh writes in responsum, klal 35, siman 7, cited by the Beit Yosef in Even HaEzer siman 91, concerning one who gave a woman engagement gifts, which she then lost, after which she rebelled against him and married another man. The Rosh writes that although she holds a dowry instrument against her present husband, we do not say that she should sell it for its present value and use the proceeds to pay for the lost gifts, because with respect to her husband she would certainly waive it. See there. Yet a dowry claim is comparable to nichsei tzon barzel, and nevertheless the Rosh writes that she can waive it and that we are concerned she will do so. This contradicts the Maadanei Melech. Below in siman 424 the Tur cites this view concerning a woman who caused damage and owns nichsei tzon barzel or nichsei melog, that she should sell them for their present value. The Perishah addresses the problem and answers that the case is where those assets still exist in their original form. I do not understand this. What difference does that make? They are nevertheless fully under the husband's control, because we rule that a loan is not given for return in specie, even if the money still exists. If his intent is the Tur's statement in Even HaEzer siman 118, as the Perishah writes, there the case is one where she has the right to demand payment from her husband whenever she wishes. If so, why should she need to sell the claim for its present value? Beit din can compel the husband to pay directly under Rabbi Natan's rule, as the Rosh explicitly writes in the responsum concerning engagement gifts cited above. The words of the Rosh and Tur therefore require further study.
What appears to me is that independently of this difficulty there was a reversal in the Rosh's position. In the second chapter of Ketubot the Rosh holds that a creditor can waive a debt even where Rabbi Natan applies, whereas in his responsa he rules that he cannot waive it. This shows that the Rosh retracted his earlier view. The Tur agrees with the ruling of the responsum, which indicates that he knew it to be the later position. It therefore appears that the discussion in Bava Kamma follows the final conclusion that where Rabbi Natan applies the intermediate creditor cannot waive the claim, while the responsum in klal 35 was written before the retraction. This explains why the Tur never cites that responsum. The matter should be understood as follows. The Ramban and Ran ask about the Gemara's suggestion there that the woman should sell the ketubah to the injured party himself. The Gemara answers that with respect to her husband she would certainly waive it and the process would therefore amount merely to troubling her for nothing. But the injured party is her creditor, and under Rabbi Natan's rule the husband should be directly obligated to him, in which case she cannot waive the debt. See the Ran's strained answer. Regarding the principal ketubah itself, it appears that the Rosh holds Rabbi Natan does not apply while she remains married to her husband. This is not for the Ran's reason. Rather, such was the nature of the rabbinic enactment of the ketubah. Rabbi Natan's basic case is Reuven who lent to Shimon and Shimon who lent to Levi. Levi's true creditor is Reuven, and Reuven is Levi's direct litigant. Shimon cannot waive the debt because the personal obligation of the second debtor is transferred to the first creditor. The Shulchan Aruch rules in seif 3 that Shimon is not obligated to collect from Levi at all; Levi himself becomes the debtor of Reuven. See what I write there. If we were to say that while a woman remains married and owes money to others her husband becomes directly obligated to her creditor through Rabbi Natan, then the woman herself would be removed from the chain and the husband would owe the creditor directly. She would then effectively be without a ketubah. Although divorce may not be easy, Tosafot in Bava Kamma write that this is why one cannot simply write the ketubah instrument in another person's name, because it is forbidden to maintain the marriage when the ketubah is not in the woman's own name. The same should apply under Rabbi Natan. See what I wrote above in Tumim to siman 66 in resolution of the Rosh's words in a different context. It follows that Rabbi Natan cannot apply to the principal ketubah while she remains married. The same Sages who enacted that she must have a ketubah also determined that Rabbi Natan's rule does not displace it. The Gemara's statement concerning one who was a creditor of his brother and the brother died, where Rabbi Natan does apply even to a ketubah, is different because there the woman herself is the first creditor seeking payment of her ketubah. That is straightforward. But this resolves only the principal ketubah. What of the additional ketubah? The Gemara concerning a woman who injured others implies that even when her ketubah exceeds the Torah minimum her creditor still cannot recover by purchasing the excess, because she could waive it to her husband. Yet under the conclusion that Rabbi Natan prevents waiver, why should this be so? We must say that the Rosh holds Rabbi Natan does not apply to a gift, and the additional ketubah is a complete gift. There is therefore no difficulty. This answers the additional ketubah. The dowry, however, which is nichsei tzon barzel, is a genuine debt. Rabbi Natan therefore applies and she cannot waive it. The Ramban's question then becomes a powerful proof: she should sell the dowry claim to the injured party and would be unable to waive it. Therefore the Rosh and Tur write below that she should sell the nichsei tzon barzel. Although the Tur's wording implies that she may sell to another person, while according to what I have written the protection against waiver exists specifically if she sells to the injured party himself, this is not difficult. Even if she sells to another, the injured party can transfer his claim to that buyer through maamad sheloshtan, or beit din can compel the woman to execute an instrument in favor of the injured party, who can then sell the ketubah claim to the purchaser for its present value. The purchaser is then secure because the woman cannot waive the claim, since she is indebted to the injured party through Rabbi Natan. When the Gemara says she should sell it to the injured party, it includes one who derives his power from the injured party. There is no difference between the injured party himself and his successor in right. This is what the Tur and Rosh intended. The explanation is clear and correct for halachah. By contrast, the responsum in klal 35 was written before the Rosh's retraction, when he still held that even a claim subject to Rabbi Natan could be waived. He therefore wrote that there was no effective solution through sale of the dowry instrument, because with respect to her husband she would certainly waive it. This is satisfactory. It follows from the Rosh and Tur that Rabbi Natan's rule does not apply to a gift. This resolves all the preceding difficulties in a correct and clear manner. The Sema in seif katan 2 likewise appears to hold that a gift is not governed by Rabbi Natan. See there. The practical halachah therefore still requires study.
Whether by way of wages. Many have wondered about the Rambam. In the first chapter of Kiddushin the Gemara says that according to the one who accepts Rabbi Natan's rule, the verse concerning the grant to a Hebrew servant, "you shall grant to him," excludes a creditor, so that the grant is given to the servant and not to his creditor. But according to the one who elsewhere also rejects Rabbi Natan's rule, the word "to him" is needed to exclude one who sold himself into servitude, who does not receive a grant. The Rambam rules like Rabbi Natan, yet nevertheless also rules that one who sold himself does not receive a grant. He appears to combine two incompatible approaches. This is especially difficult because he also rules that the grant is given to the servant and not to his creditor, writing explicitly that the creditor has no right at all in the grant. The Shach and other authorities answer that the Rambam sees no necessary connection between these rules. Although we rule like Rabbi Natan, the verse is not needed to exclude the creditor from the grant because the grant is in the nature of a gratuitous benefit and charity. The Sema calls it a concession and gift. Rabbi Natan's rule therefore does not apply, and the word "to him" can instead exclude one who sold himself. This is the essence of their answer. The reasoning is sound in itself, but a difficulty remains. The Gemara explicitly equates the matters and says that the interpretation depends on whether Rabbi Natan's rule applies. How can we introduce a distinction that the Gemara itself did not accept? What do we know that the Gemara did not? It appears that the Rambam can be reconciled as follows. In ordinary debts, the assets of the final borrower are certainly subject to the second creditor. Since that creditor himself owes the first creditor, the final borrower's assets become subject to the first creditor just as though the second creditor had sold his debt to the first creditor. Indeed, a statutory lien is stronger than an ordinary sale. Therefore one may collect from one debtor and give to the creditor of that debtor. A servant's termination grant is different. Although beit din compels the master to make the grant, the master's assets are not thereby encumbered to the servant. It is merely a mitzvah incumbent upon the master personally. Rabbi Natan therefore does not ordinarily apply, for what lien exists here that could pass to the servant's creditor? Nor have we found that the master's person itself becomes directly obligated to the servant's creditor merely because of this mitzvah, and there is no reason to assume such a rule without proof. Thus no verse is required to exclude the creditor. This works according to the view that property liens are of Torah origin. According to the view that liens are not of Torah origin, however, even an ordinary debt creates no Torah lien on property. Payment of a creditor is simply a mitzvah incumbent on the debtor personally, as is clear in Ketubot according to Rav Pappa. Yet Rabbi Natan is still derived from the verse "and he shall give it to the one to whom he is liable." We must therefore say that the Torah imposed the personal obligation of the second debtor directly toward the first creditor. The Rashba explicitly writes this at the end of Kiddushin according to the view that liens are not of Torah origin. On that premise, the servant's grant is comparable, because it too is a mitzvah incumbent personally on the master, and beit din compels him to perform it just as with payment of a debt. Without the exclusion "to him," we could therefore have compared it to an ordinary debt and said that the master's personal duty is redirected to the servant's creditor. This is satisfactory. The entire sugya in Kiddushin follows Abaye. Abaye is the one who introduced the proposition that everyone derives the gezeirah shavah from "hired servant" to "hired servant," and that the dispute instead concerns whether "to him" excludes the creditor and whether Rabbi Natan applies. Without Abaye, one might simply have said that they disagree whether that gezeirah shavah is made at all. Abaye follows his own position that property liens are not of Torah origin, as Tosafot explicitly write in Gittin 50. Thus according to Abaye the grant is indeed comparable to an ordinary debt. But since we do not rule like Abaye on this point, and we hold that property liens are of Torah origin, a servant's grant is not comparable to an ordinary debt. The phrase "to him" is therefore not needed to exclude the creditor under Rabbi Natan and may instead exclude one who sold himself. Nevertheless, the independent rule that the creditor has no right in the servant's grant remains valid. The Rambam's rulings are thus well understood. There is a second way to explain this. From the Rambam's language it appears that when we say the grant belongs to the servant and not to his creditor, we mean that even after the servant actually received the grant, the creditor has no right to seize it. The Shach likewise says that the Rambam compares the grant to poor-tithe funds, from which the Rambam rules that a creditor cannot collect. This must concern funds that have already reached the poor person, since before that they are property with no specific claimant. The Maharit in his novellae to Kiddushin makes the same inference from the Rambam's wording that "the servant's grant belongs to himself and not to his creditor," and the Mishneh LaMelech similarly infers from the Rambam's commentary to the Mishnah in the first chapter of Kiddushin, where he writes that the servant's grant belongs to him and his creditor has no right in it and may not collect his debt from it. Everyone wonders: if so, how can this rule depend on Rabbi Natan? Rabbi Natan concerns collection directly from the second debtor to the first creditor. Once the intermediate creditor has already collected his own debt, it is obvious that his creditor can ordinarily collect from him. Yet with a servant's grant, even after the servant received it, the creditor cannot seize it. It would therefore seem obvious that the exclusion "to him and not to his creditor" is necessary according to everyone. This requires explanation. The previous answers are all strained. It therefore appears that when the Rambam says that even after the servant received the grant his creditor has no right in it, he means that beit din does not descend upon those funds and seize the grant in payment of the debt, as the Mishneh LaMelech explains. The grant itself was never encumbered to the creditor. But certainly the servant remains personally obligated to satisfy his debt if he has means beyond what is protected for basic support. What difference does it make whether those means came from this source or another? Payment of a debt is a mitzvah, and if he has the ability to pay, why should he refrain? This is straightforward. According to the view that property liens are of Torah origin, therefore, where ordinary property is encumbered to the creditor, the verse "to him and not to his creditor" is meaningful with respect to the grant: it teaches that the grant itself is not encumbered, beit din does not seize it, and it cannot be distrained. According to the view that liens are not of Torah origin, however, no ordinary debtor's property is itself encumbered. There is only a personal mitzvah upon the debtor to pay, as Rashi explains in Ketubot and the Rashbam at the end of Bava Batra. What then would "to him and not to his creditor" teach regarding the grant's property status? No verse is needed, because no property is directly encumbered anywhere. As to the personal obligation of the servant himself, that certainly remains, because he is an ordinary debtor and payment of a debt is a mitzvah. The verse must therefore teach that the master himself is not directly obligated to the servant's creditor. That in turn depends on whether the second debtor generally becomes directly obligated to the first creditor, namely Rabbi Natan's rule. This explains Abaye, who holds that liens are not of Torah origin, as stated. For him, the dispute over "to him and not to his creditor" properly tracks the dispute about Rabbi Natan. But according to our ruling that liens are of Torah origin, "to him and not to his creditor" can bear its ordinary meaning, that even when the grant reaches the servant it is not itself encumbered to the creditor. That interpretation does not depend on Rabbi Natan at all. Even if the halachah were not like Rabbi Natan, we would still derive "to him and not to his creditor," as the Rambam rules. The dispute about one who sold himself then turns on whether the gezeirah shavah from "hired servant" to "hired servant" is derived. We rule that it is not, and therefore one who sold himself does not receive a grant, as the Ritva explains. This is satisfactory, and the Rambam's rulings are clear and well reconciled.
Furthermore, the first difficulty raised by the Shach and the other authorities can be answered another way. In the dispute between Rabbi Natan and the Sages whether one takes from one debtor and gives to the creditor of that debtor, the commentators ask for the Sages' rationale. Is this not merely avoiding a circular transfer? If the intermediate creditor collects, his creditor will immediately take the money from him. Why require this pointless sequence? They answer that the Sages hold we do not apply the principle that a needless circular transfer should be avoided. The second debtor can say to the first creditor, "You are not my litigant." Rabbi Natan alone teaches through the verse that the circular transfer may be bypassed. The Rashba writes this in the first chapter of Kiddushin. At the end of Kiddushin, however, it appears that in the debtor's lifetime there may in truth be no practical difference, because the circularity argument applies regardless. The distinction appears after death. If orphans collected land in payment of a debt owed to their father, their father's creditor may collect that land from them only because it was subject through Rabbi Natan, as Pesachim states. Without Rabbi Natan, the heirs could argue that they acquired the land as purchasers and that the creditor has no claim against it. Thus there is a substantial practical difference between the Sages and Rabbi Natan after death. According to this latter explanation, during the debtor's lifetime even the Sages would agree that one can collect directly. Consequently, with a living Hebrew servant there is no disagreement between the Sages and Rabbi Natan, and the phrase "to him" is needed according to everyone to exclude the creditor from the grant. If so, why would the master not be obligated? The answer must be, as above, that even after the grant reaches the servant the creditor has no specific right in that grant. There is no circular-transfer argument. One who holds that a self-sold servant receives no grant cannot therefore derive that rule from "to him"; rather, he must hold that the gezeirah shavah of "hired servant" is not derived. But according to the first explanation, that even during life the Sages reject the circularity principle, one may say that the authority who excludes a self-sold servant follows the Sages, for whom one does not ordinarily collect directly anyway, making it reasonable to use "to him" for the self-sold servant. Abaye follows his own position. In Pesachim he holds that the creditor acquires retroactively. According to him, orphans who collected land are liable to their father's creditor even without Rabbi Natan, as the Gemara there explains. Therefore he cannot use the second explanation that the dispute concerns only the effect after death. He must say that Rabbi Natan and the Sages disagree already during life over whether the circular transfer is bypassed. It follows that according to Abaye the interpretation "to him and not to a self-sold servant" can indeed depend on the dispute between the Sages and Rabbi Natan, as stated. But according to our ruling that a creditor acquires only from the time of collection, and given the general principle throughout the Gemara that a pointless circular transfer is bypassed, as the Rashba says is implied by the sugya at the end of Ketubot, the disagreement can be understood as concerning the post-death case. During life all agree that one collects directly. The phrase "to him and not to his creditor" is therefore needed according to everyone. The authority who denies a grant to one who sold himself must then do so because he does not derive the gezeirah shavah. These are precisely the Rambam's rulings. This is satisfactory. Consider this carefully.
And the interest that accrued on it. The Shach, in seif katan 4 and at greater length above in siman 72 seif katan 162, holds that if interest was fixed with a non-Jew for a year and collateral was taken for that year, then even though the non-Jew may redeem the collateral and discharge the debt before the year ends, thereby stopping future interest, the Jewish creditor nevertheless acquires a right to the interest through the end of the pledged term. This does not appear correct. The Rashba's proof in his responsum is from the case of one who undertakes to support his wife's daughter for five years, where she may collect support even from encumbered property. What proof is there if, in the collateral case, the non-Jew may redeem early? The Shach says that even in the support case, where the undertaking is only "so long as you remain with me," the daughter collects from encumbered property even though the husband has the power to divorce the mother. But there is no comparison. There, purchasers cannot say, "We divorce your wife." She remains securely married to her husband, and so long as he does not divorce her the daughter's lien remains in force. Here, by contrast, the later Jewish creditor who stands in the non-Jew's shoes can say, "I will discharge you now." What difference is there between the non-Jew himself and one who comes through him? The later Jewish creditor, as creditor of the non-Jew's creditor, proceeds through Rabbi Natan, and his legal power is the same as that of the non-Jew. Therefore the Bach is clearly correct. The Rashba's responsum concerns only interest that had already accrued before the second Jewish creditor sought to discharge the earlier creditor. In the actual case before the Rashba there was no collateral. Rather, there were an earlier and a later creditor. The later creditor came to collect and argued: how can you take interest that accrued day by day when I lent in the meantime, so that my principal debt predates the interest that accrued afterward? From this the Rashba proves from the case of daughters' support that they collect from encumbered property even when purchasers acquired the property before the five years ended, provided the support obligation had already been fixed. The purchasers remain liable for the support throughout the full five years.

urim_vetumim_urim.he:
מוציאין מלוי ונותנים לראובן ולא יכול לוי לומר לאו בע"ד דידי את דילפינן מקרא ונתן לאשר אשם לו ואפילו למ"ד שעבודא לאו דאורייתא מ"מ גוף הלוה השני משועבד למלוה ראשון כמו למלוה שלו ועיין רשב"א סוף מס' קדושין:
ל"ש נתחייב לו אחר כך ועיין מש"ל בתומים כי דין זה בצ"ע כי במחלוקת שנויה וע"ש באריכות ס"ק י' וכתבתי אם נתחייב לוי לשמעון אחר שלוה שמעון מראובן ומחל שמעון ללוי י"ל קים ליה דמהני מחילה והוא דלא כתב שמעון לראובן דאקני ע"ש:
בכל ענין שיתחייב וכו' ועיין תומים אם אינו חייב רק בתורת מתנה דצ"ע אי חל דר"נ ע"ש:
שיתחייב וכו' ואם מוציאין מלוה שחייב למסור ויתן לנמסר דעת מהרש"ל דתלי' אי דינא דגרמי דינא או קנסא. דלמ"ד קנסא הוא דרבנן לא אמרינן ביה מדר"נ והש"ך חולק דאף בדרבנן אמרינן דר"נ ועיין מה שכתבתי בתומים:
שכירות אבל מה שנתנו לו בדרך חנינה וצדקה אין מוציאין מדר"נ ומשמע אפילו הגיע כבר ליד הלוה אין למלוה זכות בו ועיין תומים סק"ג דנראה דפירש דאין המעות משועבד ואין יורדים לנכסיו אבל מ"מ אקרקפתא דגברי מוטל חיוב הפרעון אם יש ביכולתו יותר מכדי סידור ב"ח דעכ"פ חיוב מצות פרעון עליו:
ורבית שעלה עליו ודעת הש"ך דאם הלוהו לשנה בכך רבית והתנה עם הגוי שאם ירצה לפדותו תוך שנה שינכה רבית ועכשיו בא ישראל לפדותו צריך ליתן לישראל הראשון כל הרבית מכל השנה ואני כתבתי בתומים דלא נראה כן רק נותן כפי הזמן אם לא שאין רשות ביד גוי לפדותו אזי צריך ליתן רבית מכל השנה אף דמסלקו באמצע השנה:
וגובה חובו מהמותר משום דמשכון משועבד לשמעון מדר"נ ודווקא שלא יש לחוש שיגיע עי"כ אחריות והיזק לראובן סמ"ע:
urim_vetumim_urim.en:
We take from Levi and give to Reuven. Levi cannot say, "You are not my litigant." We derive the rule from the verse requiring payment to the person to whom the ultimate liability is owed. Even according to the opinion that a general property lien is not Torah law, the second debtor's personal obligation is nonetheless subordinated to the first creditor just as it is to his own immediate creditor. See Rashba at the end of Kiddushin.
There is no distinction whether he became obligated to him afterward. See what I wrote above in Tumim. This ruling requires study because it is disputed. I wrote in seif katan 10 that if Levi became obligated to Shimon only after Shimon had borrowed from Reuven, and Shimon then waived Levi's debt, Levi may be able to claim that the waiver is effective, provided Shimon had not written Reuven an after acquired property clause. See there.
In every manner in which he becomes obligated, etc. See Tumim. If Levi's obligation arises only by way of a gift, it requires study whether Rabbi Natan's rule of direct collection applies. See there.
In which he becomes obligated, etc. Where a party who caused actionable financial damage becomes obligated to pay, Maharshal holds that collection through Rabbi Natan depends upon whether liability for indirect damage is true law or merely a rabbinic fine. If it is only a rabbinic fine, Rabbi Natan's Torah rule does not apply. The Shach disagrees and holds that Rabbi Natan's collection applies even to rabbinic monetary obligations. See what I wrote in Tumim.
Wages. But money given to the debtor as charity or gratuitous support is not collected through Rabbi Natan's rule. The wording implies that even after such money actually reaches the debtor, the creditor has no proprietary lien in it. See Tumim, seif katan 3. It appears that the meaning is only that the funds themselves are not directly liened and beit din does not descend to them through Rabbi Natan, but the debtor personally remains obligated by the mitzvah of repaying debts if he has more than the protected minimum left for his needs.
And interest that accrued upon it. The Shach holds that if a Jew lent money to a non Jew for a year at a stated amount of interest, and stipulated that if the non Jew redeemed the loan early the interest would be reduced proportionately, then when another Jew comes to redeem the collateral through Rabbi Natan he must nevertheless pay the first Jew the full year's interest. I wrote in Tumim that this does not appear correct. He should pay only according to the elapsed time, unless under the agreement the non Jew himself had no right to redeem early. In that latter case the full year's interest must be paid even if the Jewish claimant removes the collateral in the middle of the year.
And he collects his debt from the excess. The reason is that the collateral itself is subordinated to Shimon through Rabbi Natan's rule. This applies only where doing so will not expose Reuven to liability or other loss. Sema.

mechaber.he: בד"א כשאין לשמעון נכסים ליפרע ממנו שסידרו לו ב"ד והשביעוהו ולא מצאו לו אלא חוב זה (אע"פ שיש לו נכסים במדינה אחרת) (ריב"ש סי' שנ"ג) אבל אם יש לו במדינה זו נכסים אין ב"ד נזקקים להוציא מזה ולתת לזה:
mechaber.en: This rule applies where Shimon has no other property from which payment can be collected, after beit din has arranged the property he is entitled to retain, made him swear, and found no asset except this debt, <small>even if he has property in another country.</small> If he has property in this country, however, beit din does not intervene to extract the debt from this third person and give it to the creditor.

baer_hetev.he: נזקקים. דזה נקרא משועבדים ואין מגבין מהם במקום שיש ב"ח אף שהגיע ז"פ החוב כן מוכח בהר"ן ולאפוקי ב"י וד"מ עכ"ל הסמ"ע ועיין בש"ך שהאריך בהרבה ראיות להוכיח דאף דאית נכסים לשמעון מ"מ נשתעבד לוי אא"כ שיש ללוי הפסד בזה כגון שאומר ששטרו של שמעון הוא פרוע או אמנה ושאר דבר המבטל השטר או שמחל לו השטר או שצריך עדיין המעות לזמן מה ושמעון רוצה להניחו אצלו וכה"ג אז אין מוציאים מלוי בע"כ אא"כ אין לשמעון נכסים כלל ואז צריך ראובן לישבע ש"ד שלא נפרע אע"פ שאין לוי יודע אם נפרע כדין כל טורף משועבדים שאינו גוב' אלא בשבועה זהו קיצור תוכן דבריו וע"ש באריכות וע"ל סימן ק"ו:
baer_hetev.en: We proceed against them. The Sema explains that this property is considered encumbered property and is not collected where the debtor has unencumbered property, even though the due date of the debt has arrived. This follows from the Ran and excludes the view of the Beit Yosef and Darkei Moshe. The Shach, however, brings many proofs that even when Shimon has other property, Levi is nevertheless directly encumbered to Reuven under Rabbi Nathan's rule. The exception is where Levi would suffer a loss, such as where he claims that Shimon's note has been paid, is a trust document, or has some other defect that voids it, or where Shimon has waived the note, or where Levi still needs the money for a period and Shimon is willing to leave it with him, or similar circumstances. In such cases we do not extract from Levi against his will unless Shimon has no property at all. If Shimon has no property, Reuven must take a Torah oath that he has not been paid, even though Levi does not know whether he was paid, just as one who collects from encumbered property may collect only with an oath. This is the substance of the Shach's discussion; see there at length. See also siman 106.

beer_hagolah.he: שם בשם בעה' בשער הנזכר וכ"ב הר"ן בפ"ב דכתובות דה"ל חוב זה כנכסים משועבדים שאין גובין מהן במקום בני חורין והכי מוכח בפרק שור שנגח ד' וה' (בבא קמא דף מ' סוף ע"א)
beer_hagolah.en: There in the name of Baal HaTerumot in the cited gate. The Ran in chapter 2 of Ketubot likewise writes that this debt is like encumbered property, from which one does not collect where unencumbered property is available. This is proved in chapter Shor Shenagach Arba'ah VaChamishah, Bava Kamma 40a.

beur_hagra.he:
בד"א. ב"ק שם הניחא כו' משום כו':
(ליקוט) בד"א כו'. עבה"ג דה"ל כמשועבדים כו' וצ"ע דא"כ במלוה ע"פ לא ליגבי ועוד דאף בשטר לא ליגבי דהא מטלטלין הוא וכמ"ש בפסחים ל"א א' אנן מטלטלין שבוק כו' וגם ראייתו אינה מוכרחת (ע"כ):
שסידרו כו' והשביעוהו. כדין משועבדים כמ"ש מגמ' הנ"ל וע"ל סי' צ"ח ס"ט ואח"כ משביעין את הלוה כו':
אע"פ שיש כו'. כמו לענין משועבדים ועבסי' קי"א סי"א וכמ"ש בכתובות פ"ח א' ורבא אמר אפי' בע"ח שלא כו' ואע"ג דאין נפרעין מן הנכסים אלא בשאין לפרוע מן האדם דנכסין אינון ערבין ליה כמ"ש בסוף ב"ב:
beur_hagra.en:
When does this apply? Bava Kamma there: "This works well..." because...
(Collected notes) When does this apply? See Beer HaGolah, which explains that it is like encumbered property. This requires study, for if so, with an oral loan he should not collect, and even with a written loan he should not collect, since this is movable property, as stated in Pesachim 31a, "We left movable property..." Moreover, his proof is not conclusive. (End of collected notes.)
When they arranged his assets... and administered an oath to him. This follows the law of encumbered property, as explained from the Gemara cited above. See below, siman 98 seif 9, that afterward they administer an oath to the borrower.
Even though there is... This is likewise the rule regarding encumbered property. See siman 111 seif 11, and as stated in Kesubos 88a, where Rava says that this applies even to a creditor who did not..., although one does not collect from property unless collection cannot be made from the person himself, because his assets are guarantors for him, as stated at the end of Bava Basra.

chelkat_mechokek.he: של פלוני הם נאמנת. אפי' שאינה נאמנת בעיני הנפקד שאומרת אמת מ"מ יעשה כדבריה דמאחר שהיא בריאה ויכולה לילך לבית הנפקד וליקח הפקדון מידו ויתן לאותו פלוני נאמנת ג"כ לומר להנפקד תן לפלוני אבל במוטלת על ערש דוי שאין לה מיגו אז יש חילוק אם נאמנת בעיניו:
chelkat_mechokek.en: She is believed to say, "They belong to so-and-so." Even if the bailee does not personally believe that she is telling the truth, he should nevertheless follow her instruction. Since she is healthy and could herself go to the bailee's house, take back the deposit, and then give it to that other person, she is likewise believed to instruct the bailee directly to give it to him. But if she is lying on her deathbed and has no such migo, then there is a distinction depending on whether the bailee personally believes her.

haggahot_imrei_barukh.he: (ש"ך הנ"ל) ואם איתא הול"ל דהיינו דוקא כו'. נ"ב צ"ע דהא דברי הרשב"א שם על דברי גמרא היכ' דל"ל נכסי מאי איכא למימר משום דאמרינן ליה כי היכא דאשתעבדנא לך כו' מזה הוכיח הרשב"א דאף בלא תבעו בב"ד ביד הלוה לשלם מעצמו מדרבי נתן:
haggahot_imrei_barukh.en: (Shach, there) And if that were so, he should have said that this applies only, etc. Note: This requires study. Rashba's words there address the Gemara's question, 'Where he has no property, what can be said?' and the answer, 'We tell him: just as I am indebted to you,' etc. Rashba proves from this that even without first being sued in beit din, the debtor may pay directly under Rabbi Natan's rule.

kessef_hakodashim.he: סעי' ה (הלך ופרע) אם תפס אחד באומרו אתה חייב לבעל חוב שלי ואח"כ תפש הבעל חוב משל הנתבע לא שייך בכך מ"ש ברס"י נ"ח שי"א שכשהשליח נפסד ע"י התפיסה אין יכול לתפוס משלו. כיון שבשעה שתפס מהנתבע הי' שייך שעבודא דר' נתן ז"ל אין גרעון על התובע ע"י מה שאח"כ גבר הבעל חוב ותפס כן י"ל מסברא ואם לא תפס רק עיקל. מכיון שתפס הבעל חוב משל מי שעיקלו משלו. לא שייך תו שעבודא דר' נתן ז"ל. ובטל העיקול ולא שייך זכי' בשביל תובע שעיקל כי הו"ל תופס לבעל חוב במקום שחב לאחרים. ואם לא תפס הבעל חוב ממון רק מטלטלי מחוסר שומא י"ל דלא נתבטל שעבודא דר' נתן ז"ל. וכ"ה כשאין החובות ברורים והכחשות ביניהם. שכיון דעומד להתברר ע"י ד"צ וע"י שבועה וקבלת חרם י"ל דלא שייך בכך סגנון איני יודע אם פרעתי מצד פרעון קודם להלואה או פקדון:
kessef_hakodashim.en: Seif 5. (He went and paid.) If a person seized property from another on the claim, "You owe my creditor," and afterward that creditor himself seized property belonging to the claimant, the rule at the beginning of siman 58, that some say an agent who suffers loss through his seizure may not reimburse himself from the principal's property, does not apply. At the moment the first seizure was made from the defendant, Rabbi Nathan's lien was in force. The claimant does not lose that right merely because afterward the creditor proved stronger and seized from him. This appears reasonable. If the claimant did not actually seize but merely obtained an attachment, once the creditor later seized the claimant's own property, Rabbi Nathan's lien no longer applies and the attachment falls away. One cannot say that the attachment already effected acquisition for the claimant, because that would be seizure on behalf of a creditor where it harms other creditors. If the creditor seized only movable property that still requires appraisal, perhaps Rabbi Nathan's lien has not yet entirely disappeared. The same may be true where the underlying debts are not clear and the parties dispute them, so that the matter remains to be determined by beit din through oath or acceptance of a ban. In such a case one should not necessarily treat the earlier payment or deposit as creating the category of "I do not know whether I paid," because the nature and extent of the debt itself remain unresolved.

ketzot_hachoshen.he:
בד"א שאין לשמעון נכסים. והוא דעת הרב' פוסקים אבל מוהרש"ל פ"ק דב"ק סי' י"ט כתב דשעבודא דר"ן אפי' אית לי' נכסי וז"ל וכ"נ מאחר דעיקר דינא דר"ן לאו מסברא קאתי אלא מקרא ושעבודא דאוריי' אית ליה גביה א"כ אין חילוק בין אית לי' נכסי בין לית ליה נכסי אבל מ"מ אין הב"ד מחוייבים להזדקק לו לעשות דין עם לוי מאחר שיש לשמעון נכסים וכו' אבל מ"מ אם תפס לוי בעבור חוב שיש לו על שמעון אפי' אית ליה נכסי לא מפקינן מיניה ונפקא מיניה שאם אותו החוב הוא בשטר אף שיש לשמעון נכסי' לא יוכל למחול ללוי שכל נכסיו משועבדים לבע"ח עד שישלם לו עכ"ל ועיין ש"ך שהאריך בזה ודעתו כדעת מוהרש"ל דשעבודא דר"ן אפי' אית לי' נכסי אלא דאם מוחל תו אין המלו' מפיק מיניה משום דכל דאיכ' פסידא ללוה כגון ששמעון הרויח לו הזמן או מחל לו דאז אין נפרעי' מנכסי' משועבדי' במקום שיש נכסי' ב"ח אפי' הן זיבורית מפני תיקון העולם אבל היכא דליכ' פסידא לשמעון אז צריך לשלם לראובן אפי' אית לי' לשמעון נכסי ונפקא מיניה דאם יש לשמעון זיבורית וללוי בינונית ולוי רוצה לשלם גובה ראובן הבינונית א"נ היכ' דלית לי' לשמעון אלא קרקע וללוי יש לו מטלטלין או מעות ורוצה לשלם דגובה ראובן המטלטלין דל"א כיון שראובן הלו' לשמעון יהי' הוא בע"ד של שמעון ולא יגבה אלא קרקע זיבורית אלא כי היכי דמשתעבד לוי לשמעון ה"נ משתעבד לראובן מדר"נ ולא מצי למימר לאו בע"ד דידי את ע"ש באורך לענ"ד נרא' כדברי מוהרש"ל דמ"ש בש"ך דהיכ' דאיכ' פסידא יכול הוא למחול משום דאין נפרעין מנכסים משועבדים במקום שיש נכסים ב"ח הנה לפמ"ש בס"ק א' ובסי' פ"ה סק"ה דשעבודא דר"ן אינו כמו שאר שעבוד נכסי דגוף של הלו' הוא ואין למלו' בהם אלא שעבוד אבל דר"ן אינו כן אלא גוף החוב הוא של המלו' ואפי' בזוזי לא מצי סלוקי ע"ש א"כ אין זה דומה להא דאין נפרעין מנכסים משועבדים במקום שיש נכסים ב"ח דהתם גוף הנכסים של הלוה אבל אם מכר דבר שאינו שלו ודאי אין במכיר' זו כלום ואפי' רוצה הגזלן או הלוקח לסלקו בזוזי מצי אמר אנא דידי בעינא וא"כ ה"נ כיון דגוף החוב אינו שלו אלא של המלו' אין לו כח למחול וכאחר הוא לגבי חוב זה. אמנם מדברי הרמב"ם פ"ב מהל' מלוה שכתב גבי אמנה או פרוע דאם אין לשמעון נכסים והודה לו שמעון אין משגיחין על הודאתו ומשמע דאם אית לי' נכסי שפיר מצי מחיל כבר כתב בל"מ שם דמחיל' ל"מ אפי' אית ליה נכסי אלא באמנה נאמן הוא כיון דלא חב לאחריני ומ"ש הש"ך שאם יש לשמעון זיבורית וללוי בינונית גובה ראובן הבינונית מלוי ולא מצי אמר לאו בע"ד דידי את לא נהירא לפענ"ד דודאי בכה"ג לא גבי ראובן הבינונית וראי' מהא דאמרינן סוף This applies when Shimon has no assets. Many authorities limit active use of Rabbi Natan's lien to a case where the intermediate debtor has no property. Maharshal, however, rules that the lien itself exists even when he has assets. Since the law derives from Scripture and is a Torah lien, there is no conceptual distinction based on solvency. Beit din may not be required to proceed against the final debtor while the intermediate debtor has available property, but the lien itself remains. Thus if the final debtor holds property or payment subject to the intermediate debt, the first creditor's right is not displaced merely because the intermediate debtor also owns other assets. The Shach agrees that Rabbi Natan's lien exists even where the intermediate debtor has assets, but he allows the intermediate debtor greater freedom where enforcing the lien would cause him loss. Thus if Shimon extends Levi's time or waives Levi's debt, the first creditor cannot necessarily proceed against Levi while Shimon has free assets, because creditors do not collect from encumbered property when free property is available. Where no loss results to Shimon, however, the first creditor may reach Levi directly. For example, if Shimon has only inferior land and Levi has medium quality land and is willing to pay, Reuven can collect the medium quality land from Levi. Similarly, if Shimon has only land and Levi has cash or movables, Reuven may collect those from Levi. In my view Maharshal's position is stronger. As explained above, Rabbi Natan's lien is not like an ordinary lien on assets still owned by the intermediate debtor. The body of the final debt belongs to the first creditor. If Shimon purports to sell or waive what is no longer solely his, that transaction cannot defeat Reuven. This is unlike ordinary encumbered property, where title remains with the debtor and the creditor has only a collection right. A practical distinction arises where the quality of land differs. If Shimon's debt to Reuven is secured by inferior land, while Levi's obligation to Shimon would ordinarily be paid from medium land, does Reuven receive only the weaker inferior quality right or the stronger right Shimon had against Levi? Since Rabbi Natan makes Reuven the true creditor of Levi, there is reason that the entire right Shimon possessed passes to him. Still, the extent to which the first creditor can improve his collection position through the intermediate debt requires attention to the exact strength of Shimon's own right. The essential principle remains that Rabbi Natan's lien exists by Torah law regardless of whether Shimon owns other assets. The question whether beit din initially directs Reuven elsewhere is procedural. It does not restore to Shimon a power of waiver over a debt that has already become substantively subject to Reuven.
Beit din does not attend to it. Rambam rules that the grant made to a Hebrew servant belongs to the servant himself and an ordinary creditor does not collect it. The Gemara derives "to him and not to his creditor," and says that the opposing view does not accept Rabbi Natan's rule in that setting. Rambam does accept Rabbi Natan generally, so why is the grant protected? The answer is that the Torah's special grant to a Hebrew servant has the character of charity and support. It is given for the servant's own rehabilitation, not as ordinary property to be diverted immediately to his creditor. The Torah therefore excludes the creditor from direct collection. Even if the servant has already received the grant, the creditor still may not collect it automatically, because the master's gift is presumed to be given for the servant's own support and not to satisfy old creditors. This is analogous to the rule that a donor may sometimes give property on condition that a creditor have no right in it. The Rosh explains that such a condition works because an ordinary creditor has only a lien, not present ownership of the property. According to the understanding of Rabbi Natan developed above, however, where the special lien truly applies the first creditor is treated as owning the intermediate debt itself. A donor cannot ordinarily stipulate away another person's already existing ownership. Therefore the protection of the servant's grant must be understood as a special Torah exclusion from Rabbi Natan's mechanism, comparable to charity. The grant is directed to the servant personally for his support and is not diverted to the creditor.

הראשון כמו בשאר ערב ומש"ה צריך נמי לתבוע להלו' הראשון תחלה והא דכתבו הטעם דלא משתעבד מדר"נ באית לי' נכסי משום דאין מוציאין מנכסים משועבדים במקום שיש בנ"ח ולא כתבו הטעם משום דערב אינו חייב באית לי' נכסים נראה משום דיש חילוק דין בין ערב ובין נכסים משועבדים דבערב אם הלוה אלם אפילו יש לו נכסים חייב הערב לשלם אבל בנכסים משועבדים אם יש להלו' נכסים אפי' הוא אלם אין מוציאין מנכסים משועבדים דהא אפי' גזלן אנס אין מוציאין מהמשועבדים כמבואר לקמן סי' קי"ח סעיף י"ג ואפילו להש"ך דס"ל בגזלן אנס דגובה מ"מ בהלו' אלם ודאי דאינו גובה ממשעבדי כמ"ש בחידושי ע"ש מש"ה הוצרכו לטעם דאין מוציאין מנכסים משועבדים במקום שיש בנ"ח היכא דיש נכסים בנ"ח להלו' והוא אלם ואינו רוצה לשלם דמטעם ערב הי' חייב ומטעם דאין מוציאין מנכסים משועבדים במקום שיש בנ"ח הוא פטור אמנם טעמא דאין מוציאין מנכסים משועבדים לא שייך רק היכא דאית לי' פסידא אבל היכא דל"ל פסידא חייב לשלם כשהלו' אלם אפי' כשיש לו נכסים, ונראה דהש"ך נתכוין ג"כ למ"ש ול"ק שוב מה שהקשה בס' הפלאה ובס' קצה"ח על מ"ש הש"ך אם יש להלו' הראשון זבורית ולהלו' השני בינונית דגובה בינונית משום שיעבוד דר"נ מהא דכתובות גבי ב' שהוציאו שט"ח זע"ז דאם יש לאחד בינונית ולא' זיבורית דזה גובה וזה גובה הא הבינונית משתעבדי מדר"נ ולפמ"ש ניחא כשהלו' הראשון רוצה לפרעו כ"ע מודה דאינו גובה מהלו' השני דהא אין לו רק דין ערב (אפי' קבלן יכול לדחות להמלו' לזיבורית דהלו' כשהלו' רוצ' לפרעו כמ"ש הסמ"ע סי' קכ"ט ס"ק ל"ז ובודאי שיעבודא דר"נ לא עדיף מקבלן) וראי' לזה מסעיף ה' דמי שיש לו מעות בפקדון דאינו יכול לומר טול קרקע ומשמע דוקא פקדון משום דברשותא דמרא קיימי אבל אם יש לו מעות בהלוא' יכול הלוה הראשון לומר טול קרקע אף שיש לו מעות להלו' השני ורוצ' לסלק תיכף והוא מטעם זה שהלו' הראשון יכול לומר אני אין רצוני לתבוע לוה שלי ואתה אין לך לתבוע לוה שלי כיון שאני רוצה לסלק אותך וכ"כ הרשב"א בתשוב' בהדיא וא"כ כ"ש בבינונית וזיבורית והש"ך לא כתב דינו רק היכא שהלו' הראשון אינו רוצה לשלם דגוב' מהלו' השני משום שיעבודא דר"נ וכדין ערב כמש"ל ובזה כ' הש"ך שפיר דאם יש להלוה השני בינונית וזבורית דאז שאם הי' להשני דין משועבדים לא הי' גובה רק מזבורית מש"ה כ' הש"ך ביון דלית לי' פסידא להלו' השני אין לו דין משועבדים וצריך לשלם בבינונית כמו שהי' צריך לשלם להמלוה שלו. ול"ק ג"כ מהך דפסחים דתיכף משעת הלוא' נשתעבד מדין ערב שבאם לא יהי' להלו' הראשון נכסים שישלם הוא ואפי' הלו' חי חל השיעבוד על הקרקע של הלו' השני מטעם ערב משא"כ במטלטלין של הלוה השני לא שייך שיעבודא דר"נ כמ"ש התוס' שם, וכן ל"ק ג"כ מהך דפרוזבול דהא אם יש להערב קרקע כותבים ג"כ פרוזבול ושיעבודא דר"נ הוי כמו ערב וכן ל"ק מהך דכתובות דמי שהי' נושה באחיו דשם הוי כלית ליה נכסי דהא כל נכסים משועבדים ול"ק ג"כ קושיית התומים דעיקר הוכחתם הוא דלא נימא דשיעבוד דר"נ הוא דהוי לוה הב' לוה של הראשון ממש דא"כ הי' לו לו' שנויא דשיעבודא דר"נ אפי' היכא דאית לי' נכסי אלא ע"כ דאינו רק דין ערב ולא הי' שוב יכול לו' התי' דשיעבודא דר"נ באית לי' נכסי דכיון דאין עליו חיוב לשלם משום דר"נ לא הי' לו לשלם:
netivot_hamishpat_beurim.en: When does this apply. See Shach, seif katan 5, who argues at length that Rabbi Natan's lien applies even where the first borrower owns other assets. First, since the lien is Torah law, why should it matter whether he owns assets? He also brings proof from the chapter Kol Sha'ah and elsewhere. From this he concludes that Rabbi Natan's lien exists even where the first borrower has assets, but where collection from the second borrower would cause the second borrower a loss, we do not collect from him, just as one does not collect from encumbered property when the debtor has unencumbered assets, because that would impose unnecessary loss on purchasers. Tumim asks: if the entire reason Rabbi Natan's lien is not enforced where the first borrower has assets is that we do not collect from encumbered property when unencumbered property exists, then the main proof from Bava Kamma, concerning an animal borrowed as presumed harmless, remains difficult. The Gemara does not answer that Rabbi Natan's lien applies in a case where the first borrower has assets. Yet there the custodian suffers no loss, so even if the first borrower has assets Rabbi Natan's lien should still be enforceable under Shach's distinction. The original question therefore returns. It appears that all of Shach's difficulties can be resolved by understanding Rabbi Natan's lien exactly like an ordinary property lien, which is also Torah law. With an ordinary property lien we rule that the encumbered property functions only as a guarantor, and the creditor must first sue the borrower, as explained in the Gemara and authorities. Beit Yosef and Tur cite a responsum of the Geonim that money is not taken from another source until the borrower is first demanded to pay, and only if he refuses is collection made elsewhere. Rabbi Natan's lien likewise requires the creditor first to sue the original borrower. It may even be weaker than an ordinary property lien, because ordinary encumbered property can in some circumstances be reached without first suing the borrower, as explained in siman 104 seif 2 and in Derishah and Perishah there, while under Rabbi Natan the second borrower resembles a personal guarantor and is secondary to the original borrower. We therefore cannot say that Rabbi Natan's law makes the second borrower into a direct borrower of the first creditor. If it did, the first creditor would not need to sue the original borrower first. Moreover, if the first borrower died while movable property remained in the second borrower's hands, it would not become movable property of heirs, because the second borrower is still alive and would supposedly be directly indebted to the first creditor. Rather, Rabbi Natan means that the first borrower's lien against the second borrower becomes encumbered to the first creditor just like the first borrower's other property. Those assets are only guarantors for the debtor, and so too the first borrower's claim against the second borrower is treated only as a guarantor. The land held by the second borrower is in turn security for the first borrower's claim. Consequently, one does not collect from the second borrower when the first borrower has assets, just as one ordinarily does not proceed against a guarantor while the borrower can pay. The authorities nevertheless formulated the reason as "we do not collect from encumbered property when unencumbered property is available" rather than simply saying that a guarantor is exempt while the borrower has assets, because there is a difference. A guarantor can sometimes be compelled even where the borrower owns assets if the borrower is violent or refuses to pay. By contrast, encumbered property purchased by others is generally not seized while the borrower still owns collectible property, even if he is violent. Even according to Shach's stricter position regarding a violent wrongdoer, an ordinary recalcitrant borrower does not justify immediate collection from purchasers. The authorities therefore needed the encumbered property rationale in a case where the original borrower owns unencumbered assets but refuses to pay. The guarantor rationale alone might have required payment, while the rule protecting encumbered property exempts the second borrower. This protection, however, applies only when payment by the second borrower would cause him a loss. If he suffers no loss, he must pay when the original borrower refuses, even though the original borrower owns assets. It appears that this is also Shach's intent. This resolves the questions of Hafla'ah and Ketzot HaChoshen on Shach's ruling that if the first borrower has only inferior land while the second borrower has medium land, the creditor may collect the medium land through Rabbi Natan's lien. They ask from Ketubot, where two parties have promissory notes against each other and one owns medium land while the other owns inferior land, and each collects from the other. If Rabbi Natan's lien attached to the medium land, why would the result be so? According to what I wrote, where the first borrower is willing to pay, everyone agrees that the creditor cannot bypass him and collect from the second borrower. Rabbi Natan's claim against the second borrower is only analogous to a guarantor. Even an ordinary guarantor can direct the creditor to the borrower's inferior land when the borrower is ready to pay, as Sema writes in siman 129 seif katan 37, and Rabbi Natan's lien is certainly no stronger than a guarantor. Proof is found in seif 5. Where the first borrower has cash held as a deposit, he cannot tell the creditor to take land instead, specifically because a deposit remains in the owner's domain. The implication is that if the cash is merely owed to him as a loan by the second borrower, the first borrower may discharge the creditor with land even though the second borrower has cash and is prepared to pay immediately. The first borrower can say, "I do not wish to collect from my borrower, and you have no independent right to collect from him while I am prepared to satisfy you." Rashba states this explicitly in a responsum. All the more so the same applies to the difference between medium and inferior land. Shach's ruling therefore concerns a case where the first borrower refuses to pay. The creditor then turns to the second borrower under Rabbi Natan, as one turns to a guarantor. In that setting, Shach correctly says that if the second borrower owns medium and inferior land, and ordinary encumbered property rules would have limited collection to the inferior land, nevertheless where paying medium land causes him no special loss he is not treated like a purchaser of encumbered property and must pay the same quality that he would owe his own lender. The proof from Pesachim is also no difficulty. From the moment of the original loan, the second borrower's land becomes conditionally encumbered like that of a guarantor, to answer if the first borrower later lacks assets. This can occur even while the original borrower is alive. Movable property of the second borrower is different, because it is not ordinarily subject to such a Torah lien, as Tosafot explain there. The proof from prozbul is likewise no difficulty, because a prozbul can be written where the guarantor owns land, and Rabbi Natan's lien functions like a guaranty. The case in Ketubot of one who was owed money by his brother is also no difficulty, because there the debtor is effectively without free assets, since all relevant assets are already encumbered. Tumim's question is likewise answered. The Gemara's proof is intended to reject the idea that Rabbi Natan makes the second borrower a direct borrower of the first creditor. If that were so, the Gemara could indeed have answered with Rabbi Natan even where the original borrower owned assets. Since the second borrower is only analogous to a guarantor, however, where the original borrower has assets there is generally no present obligation upon the second borrower to pay, so the proposed answer would not work.

netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.he:
בד"א.) ( ע"ב דעיקר דאפי' אית לי' נכסי יש על הלו' השני דין ערב שכשלא יהי' נכסי' להלו' הא' מחויב הוא לשל' וכן אם הא' אלם אפי' יש לו נכסי' מחוייב הב' לשל' ואפי' יש להא' רק זבורית ולהב' יש בינוני' זבורית מ"מ כיון שהא' אלם מחוייב הב' לשל' מבינונית או מעות אם יש לו כיון דל"ל פסיד' דהיינו שהגיע הזמן וגם אם ישל' למלו' שלו יצטרך גם כן לשלם במעות או בבינוני' מש"ה מחוייב לשלם גם להא' במעו' או בבינוני' אבל במקום דאית לי' פסידא כגון שמחל לו המלו' שלו דאז כיון דאית לי' פסידא יש להב' ג"כ דין משועבדי' ומשום הכי כשהלוה אלם ויש לו נכסי' אין השני צריך לפרוע כלל דאין נפרעים ממשועבדי' במקום שיש בנ"ח אפי' הלו' אלם ואי לית לי' נכסי להא' מ"מ א"צ לפרוע רק מהזיבורי' ואם הלו' הא' יש לו נכסי' אפי' זיבורית ורוצה לשל' אף שיש להב' בינוני' ול"ל פסידא כלל מ"מ א"י לגבות מהשני בינוני' וגובה מהא' זיבורית:
שסידרו לו. ואם המלו' השני כאן אין נפרעין עד שיודיע להמלוה השני כדלקמן סי' קכ"ט סעיף י' ש"ך:
נזקקין. ואפי' הגיע הזמן יכול הלו' לומר אפייסנו שירחיב לי הזמן:
netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.en:
When is this said? See Beurim: the primary rule is that even if the first borrower has property, the second borrower has the law of a guarantor. If later the first borrower has no property, the second must pay. Likewise, if the first borrower is violent and cannot effectively be collected from, even if he has assets, the second borrower must pay. Even if the first has only inferior land and the second has intermediate or inferior land, where the first is violent the second must pay from intermediate property or money, if he has it, provided the second suffers no loss, meaning the debt is due and he would have had to pay his own creditor in money or intermediate land anyway. But where the second will suffer loss, for example because his own lender waived the debt, then the second has the law of encumbered property. Accordingly, if the first borrower is violent but has property, the second need not pay at all, because encumbered property is not collected where free property exists, even if the debtor is violent. If the first borrower has no property, the second need pay only from inferior land. If the first borrower has property, even only inferior land, and is willing to pay, then even though the second borrower has intermediate land and would suffer no loss, the creditor cannot collect intermediate land from the second and instead collects inferior land from the first.
